extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners and patent applicants (Korea); patent attorneys and agents interacting with Korean patent examination
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining whether a claimed invention involves an inventive step (obviousness) under the Korean Patent Act, including definitions, procedure, selection of prior art, factors showing motivation/obviousness, and when advantageous effects support inventiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior to filing of a patent application (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Prior to filing of a patent application" does not refer to the filing date, but means the definite time, in hours and minutes of the filing of an application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an invention was publicly known outside Korea before the local filing time (to the hour/minute), it is considered prior art under Article 29(1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Person skilled in the art (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: "A person skilled in the art to which the invention pertains" refers to a hypothetical person who has common general knowledge in the art, ability to use ordinary technical means for R&D (experiments, analysis, manufacture), exercise ordinary creativity in selecting materials/changing designs, and comprehend all technical matters in the field at the time of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also described as an expert able to comprehend technical matters relevant to the problem solved by the claimed invention; the 'state of the art' includes common general knowledge and ordinary methods for daily work and experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention that could have been easily made (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Where an invention could have been easily made by a person skilled in the art based on an invention(s) referred to in paragraph (1)" refers to whether such a person could have easily conceived the claimed invention by exercising ordinary creativity or motivation induced from prior disclosures before filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed invention could have been easily made, it lacks an inventive step under Article 29(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental inventive step test
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining inventive step, decide whether the claimed invention could have been easily made by a person skilled in the art based on prior art references prior to filing. If yes (alone or by combining references), the claim lacks inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core obviousness test: compare claimed invention to prior art(s) from the point of view of a person skilled in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Per-claim determination
rubrics_metrics.description: When there are two or more claims in an application, the determination of inventive step should be made for each claim individually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each claim's features must be separately assessed against prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty before inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination of novelty should come before determination of inventive step; novelty and inventive step assessments are distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although notices on novelty and inventive step differ procedurally, an inventor may be notified of both grounds; Supreme Court precedent supports assessing novelty first.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner's comprehensive consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner shall consider the overall state of the art, the purpose, technical configuration, advantageous effects of the invention, and applicant arguments to comprehensively determine inventive step, focusing on the difficulty of the technical configuration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay attention to applicant arguments and assess inventive step in light of the specific purpose and effectiveness of the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three focal considerations for inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination should consider (1) whether prior art provides motivation to arrive at the claimed subject matter, (2) whether the difference is a mere exercise of ordinary creativity, and (3) whether the claimed invention has advantageous effects over prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus mainly on (1) motivation from prior art and (2) mere exercise of ordinary creativity, while considering (3) advantageous effects as supportive of inventiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for determining inventive step (steps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure: (1) specify the claimed invention (same as novelty), (2) specify scope and content of prior art references (same as novelty), (3) choose the closest prior art and clearly identify differences comparing combined elements as a whole, (4) determine whether the claimed invention could have been easily made by a person skilled in the art in view of prior art/common general knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing combined elements, treat the invention's combination as a whole rather than separated elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of prior art reference (same or relevant technical field)
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior art reference used for comparison should, in principle, be selected from the same technical field as or from a reasonably relevant technical field to the problem, effect, and use of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Same technical field typically refers to the industrial field of application but also includes fields inferred from effects/functions of elements. Prior art in different fields may be used if it can be applied to other technical fields or used in solving the claimed problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance factors when citing cross-field prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: When prior art is in a different technical field, the examiner should consider the relevance of fields, close similarity of the problem to be solved, and close similarity of function, work, or operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: container caps and closure assemblies; umbrellas and parasols; showing when cross-field citations are appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closest prior art (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The closest prior art reference" means the most relevant prior art among selected references that a person skilled in the art would choose and which discloses most of the technical features of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer prior art in proximate technical field or having the same effect, use, or addressing identical/similar technical problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach-away caution
rubrics_metrics.description: If a prior art description teaches away from the technical idea of the claimed invention, exercise care in selecting it as a prior art reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, even if a prior art teaches away, it may still be relied upon if other aspects (field relevance, similarity of function/operation) support arriving at the claimed invention (with examples combining two prior art references).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant admission of background art
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the applicant admits in the specification or written argument that background art was publicly known prior to filing, novelty can be assessed on that assumption; but if special circumstances show the admission was wrong, the assumption can be reversed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant proves special circumstances (e.g., earlier application not published as of filing, internal company knowledge not public), the examiner must remedy and continue examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing incomplete prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a prior art constitutes an incomplete disclosure (insufficient experiments or data), it can still be cited in determining inventive step if a person skilled in the art can recognize the relevant teaching.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: prior art mentioning hormone effectiveness for neurodegenerative disorders may suffice despite incomplete experimental disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probable cause or motivation grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong grounds that a person skilled in the art would have been led to the claimed invention include suggestions in prior art disclosures, close similarity of problem to be solved, close similarity of function/work/operation, and close relevance of technical fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These grounds support that the claimed invention would have been arrived at from the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggestions shown in prior art references
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggestions (explicit or implicit) in prior art disclosures relevant to a claimed invention can be strong grounds that a person skilled in the art would have been led to the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an implicit suggestion of a heat exchanger inside an airtight cooling apparatus can render the claimed feature a mere design option when combined with general technical knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Close similarity of a problem to be solved
rubrics_metrics.description: A close similarity of technical problems between the claimed invention and prior art references is a strong ground that combining prior art would be obvious to a person skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If problems differ, examiner evaluates whether the claimed problem is obvious or deducible in the field; examples include combining references for winter caps or diaphragm snap-action controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Close similarity of a function, work, or operation
rubrics_metrics.description: If close similarity exists in function/work/operation between claimed invention and prior art(s), there can be a well-founded ground that a person skilled in the art would have arrived at the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: applying a particular filter structure from an automobile filter to a home filtering apparatus when functions/operations match.

rubrics_metrics.name: Close relation of technical fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Publicly known technical means from a related technical field can be strong grounds that a person skilled in the art could have easily made the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: structures used for gloves may be applied to socks due to relation of fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere exercise of ordinary creativity (categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Common improvements based on general application of prior art, reasoning from known physical properties, or referring to other technical fields to solve known problems fall into ordinary creativity and usually negate inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical ordinary-creativity acts: selecting optimal publicly known materials, optimizing numerical ranges, replacing with equivalents, simple design modifications, partial removal of features, and simple changes/limitations of use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replacement with equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: Replacing an element with a publicly known compatible means having the same function is not inventive if it lacks an unexpected advantage; to be considered mere ordinary creativity it should be obvious at filing that the substitute is equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner may submit evidence that substitution was known as equivalent before filing. Examples: substituting SIC with Aluminum in a heat exchanger, or magnesium carbonate for oxide where known conversion occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple modification of design
rubrics_metrics.description: If an invention can be arrived at by simple design modification without changing the technical idea of the prior art and without producing advantageous effects, the inventive step is negated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Routine parameter changes (size, proportion, dimensions, amounts) are usually obvious unless they yield unexpected functional or reactive changes; examples include adjustments to microwave door protrusions or microcomputer settings for different devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial removal of technical features
rubrics_metrics.description: Omission of some technical features that are readily mentioned in prior art and whose removal predictably removes related function/effect is not inventive; inventive step may be acknowledged if omission does not affect function or unexpectedly enhances it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: omitting water-soluble silicate from toothpaste to reduce cost (and losing protective effect) is not inventive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple change or limitation of use
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim consisting merely of a use of a known invention or a further simple restriction of such use, without any advantageous effect, is not inventive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: reusing a synthetic oil as cutting oil when recycling would be naturally expected from delayed lubricating property change.

rubrics_metrics.name: General application of known art
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a known technique in a closely analogous situation to solve a prior-art problem with readily anticipated effect is not inventive; inventive step may be present if the application produces unexpected beneficial effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: transforming an administration form (pill to liquid) may be routine; forming leak-detecting holes or adopting prevalent tray types may be obvious if common practice exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantageous effects supporting inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: If an effect achieved by features defining a claimed invention is advantageous compared to prior art, it supports inventive step — especially if the effect is remarkable and unforeseeable by a person skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have recognized that unexpected advantageous effects can overcome a prima facie obviousness; this is particularly important in unpredictable fields (selection inventions, chemical inventions). Examiner may consider applicant experiment evidence or arguments if effects are inferable from description/drawings; unsupported assertions should not be considered.
